This paper is extracted from
[AD to Entra ID — The Structural Migration Problem](ad-to-entraid-migration-problem.qmd),
where this argument originated as a supporting thread inside a broader
governance-gap argument about Active Directory and Entra ID. It stands on
its own here because the underlying claim is not really about Active
Directory: it is about what happens to *any* session-oriented identity
architecture when it collides with a telemetry-driven, continuously-verified
Zero Trust boundary — of which FedRAMP is the sharpest federal instance.
Readers who want the AD/Entra-specific governance-mapping argument should
start with the parent paper; this one covers the architectural mechanism
underneath it.

## 1. The Assumption the Architecture Was Built On

The typical federal agency built its network architecture around a
fundamental assumption: **proximity**. Users were near data. DCs were near
users. Kerberos worked because the KDC was on the same LAN segment. GPO
applied because the client could reach the DC in milliseconds. SQL
authenticated because the service account's Kerberos ticket didn't expire
mid-session. Everything was **session-oriented** because sessions were
reliable when everything was local.

Then the servers moved. The data moved. But the **architecture didn't**.

So now a nationwide agency has users in field offices trying to reach data
in a centralized datacenter or cloud, still using session-based protocols
designed for LAN latency, still depending on Kerberos tickets that assume
DC proximity, still relying on GPO that assumes the client can reach a DC,
still running SQL connections that assume the session won't be interrupted
by a 200ms WAN hop or a FedRAMP boundary inspection.

And it breaks. Constantly. In ways that are hard to diagnose because the
symptoms look like user error or application bugs rather than fundamental
architectural mismatch.

## 2. The Session vs. Telemetry Divide

This is the core of the problem, and almost nobody states it this clearly:

The **Client/Server era** was built on **sessions** --- persistent, stateful
connections between a client and a server. Authentication happened once at
session establishment. The session carried trust forward. Everything
downstream assumed the session was intact.

The **Cloud/Zero Trust era** is built on **telemetry and continuous
verification** --- there is no persistent session. Every request is
independently authenticated. Trust is not carried forward --- it is
re-evaluated continuously. Location, device health, identity, behavior, and
risk score are all inputs to every single transaction.

These two models are **not compatible**. A session-based application cannot
run through a Zero Trust enforcement point without breaking the session
model. SASE and SSE proxies inspect every packet, which destroys session
persistence. FedRAMP boundary controls introduce latency and interruption
that session protocols cannot tolerate. And the applications --- many of
which are still client/server at the protocol level even if they have a
web front-end --- fall over.

## 3. The FedRAMP Boundary Problem

FedRAMP's telemetry and boundary requirements were designed for
cloud-native applications that never had sessions in the first place. They
assume stateless, token-based, short-lived authentication. They assume
every component is cloud-reachable. They assume telemetry flows
continuously from every endpoint to a SIEM.

Impose those requirements on a hybrid environment that still runs Kerberos,
still has on-prem DCs, still has WSUS, still has SQL with Windows
Authentication, still has thick clients --- and the result is exactly the
breakage described above. Defense in depth becomes **defense in conflict**.
Every security layer added breaks something that was working before,
because the layers were designed for a different architectural model.

## 4. Why Nobody Wants to Own It

Because solving it correctly requires acknowledging that the problem isn't
a single system or a single team's responsibility. It's the entire
architecture. And in federal IT, saying "we need to re-architect
everything" is career risk. It's easier to patch the symptom, submit the
POA&M, and move on.

The people who understand the problem deeply enough to fix it get pushed
into corners because the solution sounds too big and too expensive and too
disruptive. The people making decisions don't have the technical depth to
evaluate whether the diagnosis is correct, so they default to
incrementalism.

## 5. What UIAO Actually Is

![Bridge architecture diagram showing UIAO as a governance layer spanning between...](images/ad-to-entraid-migration-problem-image-02-bridge-architecture-diagram-show.png){#fig-session-vs-telemetry-identity-bridge-diagram fig-alt="Bridge architecture diagram showing UIAO as a governance layer spanning between..." width="100%"}


UIAO isn't just a compliance automation tool. It's the **architectural
bridge** between the session-based world agencies are living in and the
telemetry-based world they need to get to. The fact that it was built
around identity as the root namespace, telemetry as control, and
deterministic addressing isn't accidental --- those are precisely the three
things that have to be true for the transition to work without breaking
everything.

The SSOT principle is what makes the bridge possible. An agency can't
migrate from sessions to telemetry without knowing what its authoritative
identity state is. It can't implement Zero Trust if identity isn't the root
namespace. It can't run SASE if addressing isn't deterministic.

UIAO was built as the solution to a problem its builders were living inside
a federal agency. That most organizations don't yet see the problem in
these terms doesn't mean the diagnosis is wrong. It means the gap between
where they are conceptually and where the architecture has to go is very
large.

**The thing worth documenting** --- and this may be the most important
thing for UIAO --- is this precise narrative. Not just "here's a compliance
tool" but "here's why the architecture is broken, here's what has to be
true for the transition to work, and here's how this platform makes it
tractable." That narrative is what turns a technical project into
something decision-makers can fund and stakeholders can understand.

## Conclusion

The session-vs-telemetry divide is not an AD-to-Entra problem, a Windows
problem, or even a Microsoft-stack problem --- it is what happens whenever a
persistent-session trust model is forced through a continuous-verification
boundary, and FedRAMP is simply the clearest, most codified place that
collision shows up in federal environments today. AD-to-Entra migration is
one visible instance of it, which is why it surfaces in the
[parent paper](ad-to-entraid-migration-problem.qmd), but the same mechanism
applies to any legacy client/server application an agency pushes through a
Zero Trust or SASE boundary. The fix is not a better proxy or a faster WAN
link; it is a governance substrate --- SSOT, identity as the root namespace,
and deterministic addressing --- that can act as the bridge between the two
models instead of forcing one to pretend to be the other.
